notes.meaning: Joshua gathered all the tribes of Israel and their leaders at Shechem for one final meeting. Shechem was a sacred place where God had first promised the land to Abraham and where Jacob had buried his family's idols. Gathering there reminded everyone of God's long-standing promises to their family line.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that the entire ceremony at Shechem follows the pattern of an ancient Near Eastern covenant treaty, beginning with the ruler gathering his subjects to hear the terms.

notes.meaning: Joshua spoke directly for God, like a prophet delivering God's own words. He reminded the people that their ancestors, including Abraham's father Terah, once lived beyond the Euphrates River and worshipped false gods. God's special bond with Israel began with pure mercy toward idol worshippers, not because their ancestors were better than anyone else.

God took Abraham out of that land of false gods and guided him safely across the land of Canaan. He gave Abraham many descendants just as He promised, starting by giving him Isaac when having a child seemed impossible. Every step of their family story began with God taking the initiative.

God gave Isaac two sons, Jacob and Esau, and gave Esau the hill country of Mount Seir to live in. Giving Seir to Esau cleared the way for Jacob's line to be the sole heirs of Canaan. Jacob and his sons then went down into Egypt, where God kept them together until the right time came to fulfill His promise.

God sent Moses and Aaron to confront the Egyptian king and demand Israel's release. He struck the Egyptians with ten terrible plagues to break their grip on His people. Afterward, He led Israel out of that brutal slavery with great power.

God brought their ancestors out of Egypt until they reached the edge of the Red Sea. The Egyptian army chased after them with chariots and swift cavalry, trapping them against the water. God set the scene so His people would have to trust entirely in Him.

When the people cried out in fear, God placed a thick pillar of dark cloud between them and the Egyptian army to protect them. Then He pulled the sea over the pursuing soldiers, and the older men present at Shechem had seen that rescue with their own eyes. Afterward, God cared for the nation through forty long years in the desert.

God brought Israel to the east side of the Jordan River, where the Amorite kings Sihon and Og attacked them. God handed those kings over to Israel so the people could wipe out their armies and settle that territory. The victory belonged to God, who cleared out dangerous enemies before His people.

Balak the king of Moab tried to destroy Israel not with swords, but by hiring Balaam to put a spiritual curse on them. God refused to listen to Balaam's wishes and forced him to speak blessings over Israel time after time instead. In this way, God rescued His people from unseen spiritual traps.

Israel crossed the Jordan River on dry ground and reached the fortified city of Jericho. Jericho and all seven warlike tribes of Canaan resisted them, but God delivered every single one into Israel's hands. No fortress or alliance could stand against the Lord.

God drove out the enemy kings ahead of Israel by sending the hornet to panic and scatter them. Israel won their battles, but the credit did not belong to their own bows or military weapons. God reminded them that their victory was entirely a gift from His hand.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars view the hornet as a figure of speech describing overwhelming panic and dread sent by God, rather than swarms of actual stinging insects.

notes.meaning: God gave the Israelites a fertile land they never worked to clear, and walled cities they never built. They were now eating fruit from olive groves and grapevines that other people had planted years before. Everything they enjoyed was an undeserved gift from God's generous hand.

Because God had been so good to them, Joshua urged the people to revere the Lord and serve Him with sincere, undivided hearts. He ordered them to throw away any statues of false gods their ancestors had carried from Babylon or Egypt. Serving the true God requires tossing out every secret rival.

Joshua challenged the people to decide openly whom they would serve if loyalty to the Lord felt like too heavy a burden. They could pick the old Mesopotamian idols or the local Canaanite gods, but they had to make a real choice. Joshua then took a firm stand for himself, declaring that he and his household would serve the Lord alone.

The people answered with horror at the thought of abandoning the Lord for worthless idols. They listed how God had freed them from Egyptian slavery, shielded them on the road, and cleared the Canaanites out of the land. Because of all those mighty deeds, they declared that they too would gladly worship and serve the Lord.

Joshua startled the crowd by telling them they were not able to serve the Lord on their own strength. God is utterly holy and jealous, meaning He tolerates no rivals and will not overlook deliberate rebellion. Joshua wanted them to realize that casual promises are not enough for a holy God.

Joshua warned that if they walked away from the Lord to worship foreign idols, God's attitude toward them would change from blessing to severe judgment. He would bring ruin on them, even after all the kindness He had shown them in the past. Turning away from God brings disaster.

The people refused to back down from their commitment and insisted that they would indeed serve the Lord. They understood the high cost and still chose God over the idols. Joshua's tough warning pushed them to make a deliberate, conscious promise.

Joshua told the people that their own spoken words would stand as legal evidence against them if they ever deserted God. The crowd readily agreed, accepting that their own testimony would condemn them if they broke faith. They willingly bound themselves to their promise.

Joshua demanded that they put their promise into practice right away by destroying any hidden foreign idols. Words were not enough; they had to turn their inner desires and loyalties entirely toward the God of Israel. True devotion always shows up in outward obedience.

The people repeated their pledge a third time, promising to serve the Lord and obey whatever He commanded. Stating their choice three times gave their vow the strongest possible legal and spiritual certainty. They committed themselves fully to walk in God's ways.

Joshua formalized this renewal of the covenant between God and the nation that day at Shechem. He wrote down the rules and laws so the people would clearly know what was expected of them. A covenant is a sacred agreement where God binds Himself to His people and calls for their loyalty.

Joshua recorded these covenant words in the Book of the Law of God, adding to the sacred scrolls started by Moses. Then he set up a large standing stone under a grand oak tree near the holy meeting place of the Lord. The massive stone stood in plain sight so everyone would remember what happened.

Joshua told the crowd that this stone would act as a silent witness against them if they ever turned away from God. He spoke poetically of the stone having heard everything God said and all the vows the people had made. Its silent presence would constantly remind them to keep their word.

Having completed the covenant ceremony, Joshua sent all the families back to their allotted lands. Each tribe returned home with a fresh reminder of their duty to God. Joshua's public leadership of the entire nation was now complete.

Not long after this great assembly, Joshua died at the age of 110. Scripture honors him with the noble title of servant of the Lord, an honor previously given to Moses. He reached the end of a long life having faithfully finished the work God gave him.

The Israelites buried Joshua on his own family property at Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim. He was laid to rest north of Mount Gaash in the very land he had helped conquer and divide. His peaceful burial in the promised land showed that God's gift of rest had truly arrived.

Israel remained faithful to the Lord throughout Joshua's lifetime and during the lives of the older leaders who survived him. These leaders had personally seen the miracles God performed from Egypt to the conquest. Their living memories helped keep the nation steady and true to God's ways.

The Israelites buried the bones of Joseph at Shechem, fulfilling the dying wish Joseph had made centuries earlier in Egypt. They placed him in the field Jacob had bought for one hundred pieces of silver, which became part of the inheritance for Joseph's descendants. Joseph's burial proved that God keeps His promises across many generations.

Eleazar the high priest, Aaron's son, also died and was buried on the hill given to his son Phinehas in Ephraim. Eleazar had stood beside Joshua to divide the land and lead the nation in worship. With the burials of Joshua, Joseph, and Eleazar, an entire founding generation rested safely in the land God had promised them.
